Learning Objectives
Identify the epidemiology, etiology, risk factors, and injuries associated with displaced
calcaneus fractures.
Review the indications for open reduction and internal fixation versus nonsurgical
management of calcaneal fractures and the respective associated risks and outcomes.
Recognize calcaneal fracture patterns requiring immediate surgical stabilization.
Describe approaches for the surgical fixation of calcaneal fractures, including their indications,
advantages, and disadvantages.
Describe the long-term outcomes and complications of calcaneal fractures.

Overview

Overview
Historically, calcaneal fractures have been devastating injuries fraught with
complications and long-term sequelae.1 Detailed knowledge of the complex calcaneal
anatomy and limited soft-tissue envelope is mandatory for successful management of
these fractures, which commonly lead to arthritis, pain, and difficulty with shoe wear.
Ideal management is a subject of controversy, and many patient and fracture factors
must be considered to limit complications and optimize outcomes.
Epidemiology
Most calcaneal fractures occur in males.
Common causes of calcaneal fractures include workplace accidents, motor vehicle collisions,
and falls.

Epidemiology
Most calcaneal fractures are secondary to high-energy axial loads, such as those
sustained during a motor vehicle collision or a fall from a height. Most injuries have an
intra-articular component typically involving the posterior facet of the subtalar joint. A
large percentage of injuries occur in young, male laborers who often experience several
years of subsequent disability.2-4

The calcaneus has a complex anatomy. Distally, the calcaneocuboid articulation is saddle
shaped and curved posterior as it extends medially.1 Superiorly, the subtalar joint
includes three separate facets that articulate with the underside of the talus in a
coordinated fashion. The posterior facet comprises the largest part of the subtalar joint
and slopes inferiorly as the joint travels medially.1 The middle facet rests on the
sustentaculum tali and supports the centromedial talar body. This region, which has
been called the constant fragment, is less displaced in calcaneal fractures; however,
more recent CT data have demonstrated involvement of the middle facet.2 The anterior
facet is located just anterior to the middle facet on the anteromedial calcaneus. The
lateral wall is relatively flat, with the exception of two prominences. The peroneal
tubercle separates the peroneus brevis from the peroneus longus as they pass along the
lateral calcaneus. Another small prominence serves as the insertion point of the
calcaneofibular ligament.5,6
The middle and anterior facets carry a higher pressure.3,4 Therefore, dense bone in this
region serves as an anchor point during internal fixation.5-7 Most of the calcaneus is
cancellous, with thicker bone supporting the posterior facet, sustentaculum tali, and
angle of Gissane—the most important regions for placement of internal fixation.6
Vascular Anatomy
The posterior tibial artery travels medially (Figure 2).
The calcaneal branch of the peroneal artery travels laterally and supplies the flap made during
an extensile lateral approach.

Vascular Anatomy
The blood supply of the calcaneus is quite rich and forms from a complex network of
collateral arteries. The relevant arteries encountered during the management of
calcaneal fractures are the calcaneal branch of the peroneal artery and the medial
calcaneal branch of the lateral plantar artery. The calcaneal branch of the peroneal
artery is located a mean distance of 22.04 mm anterior to the calcaneal tuberosity and

cadaver models, it lies within the vertical limb of the traditional extensile lateral
calcaneal approach.8 The medial calcaneal branch arises from the lateral plantar artery,
which arises from the posterior tibial artery. The medial calcaneal artery supplies most
of the blood flow to the fat pad, and damage to this artery commonly results in heel pad
necrosis and very poor outcomes.9
Neural Anatomy
Sural nerve
Tibial nerve

Neural Anatomy
The most relevant neural anatomy in the calcaneus is the sural nerve, which may
transverse the extensile lateral incision proximally and distally. This is an entirely sensory
nerve that may form painful neuromas if damaged. In the calcaneal region, the sural
nerve typically is superficial to and just inferior to the peroneal tendons.10 The tarsal
tunnel rarely is involved during calcaneal fracture management unless a large
posteromedial injury has been sustained. The tibial nerve rests posterior to the posterior
tibial artery and must be protected during medial approaches to the calcaneus.

Achilles tendon
Plantaris tendon

The Achilles tendon is formed by the junction of the gastrocnemius and the soleus
aponeuroses. It inserts broadly on the superior and posterior aspects of the calcaneal
tuberosity.
If present, the plantaris tendon inserts on the posterior superior calcaneal tuberosity
medial to the Achilles tendon insertion.
Joints and Ligaments
Subtalar joint
Calcaneocuboid joint
Plantar fascia
Calcaneofibular ligament
Bifurcate ligament

Joints and Ligaments
The subtalar joint is composed of the posterior, middle, and anterior facets. The
posterior facet forms most of the subtalar joint complex. The calcaneocuboid joint is a
saddle shaped joint at the anterior aspect of the calcaneus at the articulation with the
cuboid. The plantar fascia is an aponeurosis of thick tissue beneath the skin that begins
at the plantarmedial calcaneal tuberosity and terminates at the plantar aspect of the
proximal phalanges of the toes. The calcaneofibular ligament is part of the lateral
ligamentous complex of the ankle arising from the distal fibula and inserting on the
lateral wall of the calcaneus posterior and superior to the peroneal tubercle and lying
deep to the peroneal tendons. The bifurcate ligament arises from the superior aspect of
the anterior process of the calcaneus and inserts onto the navicular and cuboid bones.

Abductor hallucis
Abductor digiti minimi


Musculature
Most of the musculature of the calcaneus is avoided during the management of
calcaneal fractures; however, the extensor digitorum brevis and the extensor hallucis
brevis may be elevated during a sinus tarsi approach or if fixation is necessary for an
anterior process of the calcaneal fracture. The extensor digitorum brevis originates from
the dorsal lateral calcaneus and terminates as four separate tendons on the respective
middle phalanxes. The extensor hallucis brevis arises from the medial part of this same
muscle and inserts at the dorsal proximal phalanx of the great toe. The abductor hallucis
originates from the medial aspect of the calcaneal tuberosity and inserts on the medial
aspect of the great toe proximal phalanx. The abductor digiti minimi originates from the
lateral aspect of the calcaneal tuberosity and inserts on the lateral aspect of the fifth toe
proximal phalanx. The quadratus plantae originates from the plantar calcaneal
tuberosity and inserts as muscular attachments to the flexor digitorum longus. The
flexor digitorum brevis is immediately deep to the plantar fascia (aponeurosis) and
inserts on the middle phalanx of the lesser toes.
Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
Intra-articular fractures
Mechanisms of injury (Figures 3 and 4; Resource 1)
Intra-articular fractures affecting the posterior facet are most common.
The most frequent mechanism of injury in patients with an intra-articular fracture is an axial
load driving the talus into the calcaneus and propagating the fracture (Video 1).

Extra-articular fractures
As many as 20% of calcaneal fractures are extra-articular.
Management of an extra-articular fracture depends on displacement.
A displaced tongue-type fracture may compromise the posterior skin and must be urgently

Fractures of the anterior process
Avulsion fractures may be managed nonsurgically or excised.
Involvement and displacement of the calcaneocuboid joint requires ORIF.
Fractures of the sustentaculum
Isolated sustentaculum fractures are rare but may cause instability if displaced.

Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
More than 75% of calcaneal fractures are intra-articular, and most of these involve the
posterior facet of the subtalar joint. An axial load sustained during a fall from a height or
from a motor vehicle collision is the most common mechanism of injury. The lateral
process of the calcaneus is driven into the floor of the sinus tarsi, and the primary
fracture line exits posteromedial, dividing the tuberosity and the lateral wall fragment
from the sustentaculum and the anterior process fragment. The tuberosity is driven
superiorly, and the lateral wall is commonly displaced beneath the fibula. The medial
fragment includes the sustentaculum tali and is commonly known as the constant
fragment. This region has very strong ligamentous and capsular attachments, allowing it
to typically maintain near-anatomic positioning and making it a reference point for
fracture reduction. The superolateral fragment includes the posterior facet and the
posterolateral tuberosity of the calcaneus.6 Secondary fracture lines are variable and
may result in tongue-type and joint depression-type patterns in which the tuberosity is
attached or separated from the posterior facet, respectively.

Many extra-articular fractures require surgical management to minimize soft-tissue
breakdown, increase function, and allow for comfortable shoe wear11 (Video 2). The
strong-contraction gastrocnemius-soleus complex may avulse the posterior tuberosity
and may be intra-articular or extra-articular, depending on the accompanying axial load.
If superiorly displaced, these fractures can cause rapid posterior skin breakdown,
requiring urgent reduction. Small fractures may be excised, but most will require open
reduction and internal fixation (ORIF), which may be performed percutaneously,
especially in patients with an extra-articular fracture.12

The plantarmedial calcaneus is the attachment site of the heel fat pad, abductor hallucis,
and plantar fascia. Fractures in these structures typically result from a direct impact. If
the impact is high energy or accompanied by a displaced tongue-type calcaneus fracture,
substantial displacement may result, warranting ORIF. Displacement often separates the
plantar fascia from the calcaneus and may cause loss of the longitudinal arch, alteration
of the windlass mechanism, and doubling of longitudinal arch stress.13 High-energy
plantarmedial calcaneal fractures may also cause tarsal tunnel syndrome, requiring a
medial approach for reduction, fixation, and tarsal tunnel decompression14 (Figure 5).

Anterior process fractures may occur in isolation or in combination with other patterns.
In isolation, the fracture results from inversion and plantar flexion, similar to an ankle
sprain. A superolateral anterior process avulsion results from pull of the bifurcate
ligament. Small extra-articular fragments may be immobilized for 4 to 8 weeks or
excised. If displaced, larger fragments involving more than 25% of the calcaneocuboid
joint should be managed via ORIF.5
Sustentaculum fractures without involvement of the posterior facet may cause instability
of the transverse tarsal joints and the subtalar joints. Associated injuries involve the talar
neck, talar body, cuboid, and talonavicular dislocations.7 Isolated, displaced fractures of
the sustentaculum may be managed via ORIF and typically are associated with low
complication rates.7

Risk Factors
Male
Laborer
Young age

Risk Factors
Risk factors for calcaneal fractures include occupations and activities that may result in a
substantial axial load (most often, a fall from a height or a motor vehicle collision). Young
male laborers are at greatest risk for these fractures. Risk factors, such as alcoholism,
osteoporosis, and older age, may decrease bone quality, resulting in fracture from a
lesser load.5,15
Associated Injuries
Spinal burst fracture
Pelvic/acetabular fracture
Ipsilateral knee, ankle, and midfoot fractures

Associated Injuries
Calcaneal fractures may be associated with other injuries. For example, spinal burst
fractures, particularly in the lumbar region, are associated with displaced calcaneus
fractures from a high-energy mechanism of injury. All patients with a calcaneal fracture
should have their spine palpated during the initial evaluation, and a low threshold for
spinal imaging should exist. Pelvic and acetabular fractures also are associated with
calcaneal fractures, particularly those involving motor vehicle collisions. These fractures
typically are identified on routine pelvic imaging studies during the trauma workup.
Ipsilateral knee, ankle, and midfoot fractures also may occur. Although knee fractures

Injury Classification
The Sanders classification of calcaneal fractures is based on semi-coronal CT through the
widest part of the posterior facet, with the fracture type based on the number and location of
fragments. Although this classification system has been correlated with outcomes in some
studies, its reproducibility has been moderate.
The Essex-Lopresti classification system separates calcaneal fractures into tongue and joint
depression types. This classification system is useful in determining management but is not
predictive of outcomes.

Injury Classification
The Sanders classification system is the most well-known and widely used tool for
categorizing calcaneal fractures. The classification system is based on semi-coronal CT of
the widest part of the subtalar joint posterior facet5,15 (Resource 2; Figure 6). Sanders
type I fractures are nondisplaced. In type II fractures, the posterior facet is separated
into two fragments, whereas in type III fractures, the posterior facet is separated into
three fragments. Type II fractures are subclassified as type IIa, type IIb, or type IIc,
depending on if the fracture line is lateral, central, or medial, respectively. Type III
fractures are subclassified as type ab, type ac, and type bc depending on if the two
fracture lines are lateral and central, lateral and medial, or central and medial,
respectively. Type IV fractures are extensively comminuted, with more than three
articular fragments of the posterior facet.

appropriate reduction technique.

Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
A fall and a motor vehicle collision are the most common patient histories related to a
calcaneal fracture.

Patient History
Most patients with a calcaneal fracture have fallen from a height. Patients with a
displaced calcaneus fracture often are involved in high-energy injuries, such as a motor
vehicle collision. Many of these patients have multiple traumatic injuries and warrant
assessment for other sources of pain. Medical history and social factors, such as
diabetes mellitus, neuropathy, peripheral vascular disease, nicotine use, alcoholism, and
occupation, are very pertinent and may influence medical and surgical decision making.

Physical Examination
Open calcaneus fractures commonly are medial, and skin at risk of injury is commonly
posterior, near the Achilles tendon attachment.
Compartment syndrome may occur in as many as 10% of patients with a calcaneal fracture.
Although blistering typically does not occur immediately, it may be decreased via immediate
splinting and elevation.
Hemorrhagic blistering indicates a severe deep-tissue injury, and this region should be avoided
during surgical management if possible.

Physical Examination
Calcaneal fractures most commonly manifest as severe swelling and pain to the heel.
The entire foot and ankle should be examined for associated midfoot and ankle injuries.
Nonblanching skin posteriorly may indicate a displaced tongue-type calcaneus fracture
requiring immediate reduction to avoid skin necrosis. Open calcaneus fractures are
uncommon but may result from high-energy mechanisms of injury. They most often are
open medially and are associated with a high risk of nerve and vascular involvement.5 In
addition, open calcaneus fractures often are Gustilo and Anderson type III, and as many
as 50% result in osteomyelitis.12
Compartment syndrome occurs in as many as 10% of patients with a calcaneus fracture;
however, because immediate pain is expected after these fractures, compartment
syndrome often is difficult to diagnose clinically. Pain out of proportion, increasing pain
medication use, and pain with passive stretch of the toes should increase suspicion for
compartment syndrome, which can be confirmed via compartment pressure testing.17
Neurovascular Examination
The degree of soft-tissue swelling after a calcaneal fracture may limit neurovascular
assessment.


Neurovascular Examination
After a calcaneal fracture, a large amount of swelling in a relatively small area often
makes the palpation of pulses very difficult. Capillary refill should be brisk, and the limb
should be warm. Although vascular compromise is uncommon in patients with a
calcaneal fracture, a Doppler examination can be performed to verify an adequately
perfused limb if necessary. Typically, sensory examination also is diminished because of
the edema compressing the superficial nerves. Strength assessment of the foot and
ankle usually is limited by severe pain.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
Axial view (Harris): An axial view shows primary joint displacement, angulation of the
tuberosity, and any increase in heel width. This view is difficult to obtain preoperatively;
however, if obtained intraoperatively, the axial view will ensure no varus is present (Figure 8).
Böhler angle: On a lateral radiograph, a decrease in the Böhler angle is one measure of the
severity of joint injury and displacement (depression). A normal Böhler angle is 25° to 40°. If
this angle remains greater than 15°, nonsurgical management may be considered (Figure 9).
Broden views: These special oblique calcaneal radiographic projections typically are obtained
intra-operatively to show the congruence of the subtalar joint. They are taken at 30°, 50°, and
70° to the horizontal plane (Figure 10).
The initial radiographic evaluation should include a non‒weight-bearing calcaneal series
consisting of axial and lateral calcaneal views and AP and oblique foot radiographs.

Radiography
For all patients with a calcaneal fracture, radiographs should include AP, lateral, and
oblique foot views. The axial, or Harris, view reveals widening, shortening, lateral
translation, and varus positioning of the tuberosity fragment; however, a Harris view
may be difficult to obtain in patients with pain. An AP view of the ankle is useful for
assessing extrusion of the lateral wall of the calcaneus with impingement against the
fibula or peroneal tendons.
A lateral view of the foot and ankle may help determine the Böhler angle, or the
intersection of a line from the posterosuperior margin of the posterior facet to the

most superior margin of the anterior process of the calcaneus (normally 20° to 40°); this
view also may be used to assess loss of height. Double density of the posterior facet
indicates subtalar incongruity.15 The angle of Gissane parallels the lateral process of the
talus and is measured from the superoposterior facet to the anteroinferior posterior
facet and from this point to the anterior process superior point. This decreases if the
entire posterior facet is separated from the sustentaculum and is depressed. AP and
oblique foot views can detect involvement of the calcaneocuboid joint.
Broden views help evaluate reduction of the posterior facet intraoperatively. These views
are obtained with ankle internal rotation of 30° to 40° and the x-ray beam centered over
the lateral malleolus. The beam should be angled 10°, 20°, 30°, and 40° toward the head
of the patient for full evaluation of the subtalar joint. These views are most useful
intraoperatively to assess posterior facet reduction.15

Complications
Complication rates as high as 40% have been reported in fractures of the calcaneus. Factors
that increase the risk of complications include falls from a height, early surgical management,
and smoking.25 Approximately 10% of patients have associated injuries of the lumbar spine.
Nonunion
A nonunion is rare with calcaneal fractures.
Nonunion of the calcaneus after fracture is very rare; however, a few cases have been
reported. Nonsurgical management of the fracture may be a risk factor.41-45
Malunion/Malalignment
Malunion and malalignment are common after calcaneal fracture because of the complex
anatomy. Loss of height, widening of the tuberosity, lateral impingement, and posterior facet
malreduction are the most clinically relevant symptoms.

Malunion/Malalignment
Calcaneal malunion may result in loss of height, widening of the heel, lateral
impingement, or arthritis. Loss of calcaneal height results in a relatively flattened talus,
decreasing the declination angle of the talus to less than 20°, which limits dorsiflexion of
the ankle and causes anterior ankle impingement.
Impingement of the lateral wall associated with malunion may result in peroneal tendon
pathology. This injury may be managed via lateral exostectomy; however, concurrent
height collapse and subtalar arthritis are common and typically require in situ or

of the heel and loss of calcaneal height.15 Residual varus may require a lateralizing

Superolateral malalignment with overreduction of the posterior facet causes varus

Sinus tarsi approaches are capable of the same degree of reduction as extensile lateral
approaches. In a 2014 study on the sinus tarsi approach versus minimally invasive
methods, anatomic alignment of the posterior facet of the subtalar joint was achieved in
64 of 69 displaced intra-articular calcaneus fractures.47 A retrospective nonconcurrent
study found that anatomic reduction was similar between patients with a displaced
intra-articular calcaneus fracture managed via the extensile lateral approach and those
managed via the sinus tarsi approach; however, fractures managed via the sinus tarsi
approach resulted in fewer wound complications, shorter surgical times, shorter time to
surgical management, and shorter hospital length of stay.48
Settling of the posterior facet, as evidenced by a decreasing Böhler angle, occurs to a
similar degree regardless whether management is surgical or nonsurgical. Bone grafting
does not appear to reduce this risk; however, less settling may be observed at long-term
follow-up after a bone graft.21 Consensus is lacking on whether locking plates or
conventional plates are more effective at reducing or preventing settling.21,49
A missed or displaced plantarmedial fragment may cause pain and occasionally requires
exostectomy.15

Pain is common after calcaneal fracture but typically is manageable.
Acute pain out of proportion to the injury should be evaluated for compartment syndrome.

Pain is an expected sequela of calcaneal fractures, but it usually is manageable.
Calcaneal fractures typically result from a high energy applied to the bone and soft-

have reported an absence of pain in as many as 25% of patients 1 year after calcaneal

follow-up 2 to 3 years postinjury.34,39 Regardless of surgical or nonsurgical management,
pain decreases by a similar degree after fracture, and rates of long-term pain with
weight bearing are similar.20

Wound complications are common with calcaneal fractures because of the vulnerable soft-
tissue coverage.
Smoking substantially increases wound complication rates in calcaneal fractures, and
cessation should be mandatory for patients treated surgically.

fasteners along with necrotic bone.15,18 As many as 15% of patients who smoke may

Arthritis
Displaced intra-articular calcaneus fractures typically result from a high-energy
mechanism of injury, with damage to the cartilage even with anatomic reduction.
Intermittent subtalar injections may confirm the diagnosis and treat pain. University of
California Biomechanics Laboratory orthotics, walking aids, NSAIDs, and bracing also
may be helpful. If these treatment options fail, in situ fusion may be performed if no
ankle impingement is present. If height loss also is present, bone block distraction
arthrodesis is indicated.5

as much as 41% with ORIF, but this does not appear to substantially affect measured
outcomes. However, outcomes from subtalar arthrodesis are improved if patients have
undergone prior ORIF. This finding is thought to be secondary to more normalized
calcaneal geometry and a technically easier procedure.20,28,52

Ankle and subtalar instability are uncommon with ORIF and nonsurgical management of
calcaneal fractures; however, stiffness of the subtalar joint complex is common.
Avulsions of the superior peroneal retinaculum may occur after calcaneal fractures and may
cause persistent peroneal instability in surgically and nonsurgically managed calcaneus

Stiffness/Instability
Because most calcaneal fractures involve the posterior facet of the subtalar joint, more
than 75% of calcaneal fractures have some degree of limited inversion and eversion.39
Ankle instability is not common after calcaneal fracture regardless of management;
however, peroneal tendon instability may occur, affecting as many as 30% of intra-
articular displaced calcaneus fractures.53,54 Lateral wall displacement or buckling also
may displace the peroneal tendons. Some patients will have avulsion of the superior
peroneal retinaculum, which is noted as a fleck sign at the posterior distal fibula on a CT
scan. Most unstable peroneal tendons will reduce to a stable position after ORIF of the
calcaneus; however, some will require temporary K-wire fixation or splinting in
dorsiflexion and inversion. Late peroneal instability or missed dislocated peroneal
tendons may be managed via reconstruction of the superior peroneal retinaculum, often
with deepening of the fibular groove.

After a calcaneal fracture, patients are at risk for hematoma, which may cause skin necrosis,
and deep vein thrombosis (DVT).

After a calcaneal fracture, the risk of an expanding hematoma causing skin necrosis is
quite rare and must be balanced against the need for DVT prophylaxis.5 The risk of
hematoma is as high as 4.7%,51 and many surgeons recommend placement of a drain
under the flap during an extensile lateral approach to reduce the risk of skin
compromise. Conversely, in a recent study, as many as 12% of patients with a calcaneal
fracture had postoperative DVT.51 Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis should be
considered for all patients undergoing surgical management of a calcaneal fracture,
especially those with risk factors, such as older age, obesity, smoking, and previous DVT.

Neural Injury/Nerve Palsy
The nerve that is injured most often during ORIF of calcaneal fracture is the sural nerve.
Complex regional pain syndrome may occur after a calcaneal fracture regardless of

Neural Injury/Nerve Palsy
The most common neural injury related to a calcaneal fracture is damage to the sural
nerve. This often occurs during an extensile lateral approach because the sural nerve
typically lies within the vertical and longitudinal arms of this approach. Damage to the
sural nerve, which is purely sensory, may cause numbness or a painful neuroma. The
tibial nerve also may be injured from entrapment, which often is secondary to malunion
after nonsurgical management.15
Complex regional pain syndrome may occur regardless of fracture management.15 Early
identification, motion, edema control, desensitization therapy, and early referral to a
tertiary specialist are recommended for affected patients.
Compartment syndrome occurs in as many as 10% of patients with a calcaneus fracture.
It commonly leads to claw toe deformity and also may cause contracture, permanent
loss of function, weakness, and paresthesias.15
Rehabilitation
After calcaneal ORIF, aggressive motion should be initiated as soon as the wound has sealed;
after nonsurgical management of a calcaneal fracture, aggressive motion should start as soon
as soft-tissue swelling allows.
Although early weight bearing has not been shown to increase collapse of the posterior facet,
it should not be initiated until bone healing has been observed (ie, 6 to 12 weeks).

Rehabilitation
Rehabilitation after calcaneal fractures begins with edema control and avoidance of
Achilles tendon contracture. For all calcaneal fractures, a splint with compression
bandages and elevation for edema management should be applied immediately. For
surgically managed fractures, a nonremovable splint should be applied over the surgical
dressings until the wound has healed. Wound healing typically takes 2 to 3 weeks, after
which range of motion exercises usually are initiated. Patients with a nonsurgically
managed calcaneal fracture can begin range of motion exercises as soon as soft-tissue
swelling allows. Bony union takes 6 to 12 weeks, at which time progressive weight
bearing is initiated; partial–weight bearing is historically initiated between 6 and 8 weeks,
with full–weight bearing initiated between 3 and 4 months and discontinuation of a
brace between 4 and 6 months.5,15,18,20-22,32,35,39,47 Early–weight bearing (ie, as quickly
as 4 to 5 weeks postoperatively) has not increased the subsidence of subtalar joints
managed with the use of locking plates and 4.0 mm screws.55 In fact, a randomized
multicenter study found that the initiation of weight bearing at 3 weeks postoperatively
improved joint congruence and reduction, as well as patient outcome scores.29 Return
to preinjury occupation may be anticipated between 6 and 9 months, and patients can
expect near-full dorsiflexion and plantar flexion of the ankle with 50% to 75% inversion
and eversion of the subtalar joint.5
Outcomes
Outcomes after a calcaneal fracture are related to the severity of the initial injury, accuracy of
the fracture reduction, number of articular fragments, and patient condition.
Sanders type IV intra-articular displaced calcaneus fractures are associated with the poorest
outcomes.
Younger age, female sex, non‒workers’ compensation status, and lighter work duties are
associated with better outcomes after ORIF.

Outcomes of displaced intra-articular calcaneal fractures are variable and depend on
numerous factors. Therefore, to date no large, randomized, controlled trials have shown
clear benefits with ORIF versus nonsurgical management. The accuracy of reduction,
severity of the initial injury, and number of articular fragments substantially affect
patient outcomes. For example, the Sanders classification system approaches
importance in predicting outcomes. Patients with Sanders type I or type II injuries have
much better outcomes than those with Sanders type IV fractures.5,15,27 Anatomic
reduction is possible for most Sanders type II and type III fractures, whereas Sanders
type IV injuries rarely are anatomically reduced.15 A 2013 level II study comparing ORIF
with nonsurgical management of displaced intra-articular calcaneus fractures
demonstrated that ORIF was not superior at 1 year postoperatively, but it did afford
some benefits 8 to 12 years postoperatively. The risk of complications was higher with
ORIF, but the treatment also reduced subtalar arthritis. In all, 57% of fractures were
reduced to within 2 mm, and 19% of patients had infections, with one patient eventually
undergoing transtibial amputation for a methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus
infection and another patient requiring removal of instrumentation and administration
of intravenous antibiotic agents.20
The presence or absence of complications extensively influences outcome, leading many
surgeons to adopt minimally invasive approaches for complicated calcaneal fractures.
Such techniques may improve outcomes compared with the extensile lateral approach
but only if similar anatomic reductions and stable fixation are achieved.27 The poorest
outcomes are associated with surgical fixation with inadequate reduction or major
complications.4 Most studies comparing extensile lateral with minimally invasive
approaches have demonstrated similar radiographic and clinical outcomes but fewer
wound complications with minimally invasive procedures.32,37-39,47,56,57
Many patients with a displaced intra-articular calcaneus fractures are industrial workers
who may be incapacitated for as long as 3 years and partially impaired for 5 years.15
Women, younger patients, those with non‒work-related injuries, and those with lighter
workloads have much better outcomes with ORIF than with nonsurgical treatment.22

Another predictor of outcome is the Bohler angle at the time of injury. Patients with a
Bohler angle of 15° to 36°, a moderate tongue-type pattern and non‒work-related

preinjury occupation after 6 to 9 months with near-full dorsiflexion and plantar flexion.
These patients can expect between 50% to 75% inversion and eversion and should be
able to wear a normal shoe; however, some will require an orthotic.5 A retrospective
single-center study found substantial correlation between clinical and pedobarographic
results. Inferior functional outcome was associated with decreased subtalar motion,
specifically lack of eversion, which resulted in lateral load shift during gait.58
In another study, long-term evaluation (mean follow-up, 15.22 years) of 108 displaced
calcaneus fractures managed surgically found that 29% of patients required arthrodesis
for posttraumatic arthritis. Patients who did not require arthrodesis had a mean visual
analog scale score of 1.75, with scores ranging from 0 to 1 in 56% of these patients.
Functional outcomes on the Medical Outcomes Study 36-Item Short Form physical
component summary demonstrated that 77% of the nonfused group (51 of 66) were
within the US norm, 46% (30 of 66) of whom were above the norm.59
The largest study of open calcaneus fractures to date demonstrated an overall
complication rate of 23.5% in 127 open calcaneus fractures over a 12-year period; 12.2%
of fractures resulted in a deep wound infection, and 2.5% led to amputation.60 A
systematic review of 616 open calcaneus fractures found the mean time to surgical
repair was 9.8 days, with a complication rate of 21%.61

CT scans should be obtained for all intra-articular calcaneus fractures. Those that appear to be
nondisplaced on plain radiographs may have displacement of more than 2 mm on CT.
